## Introduction {#sec-introduction}

Constructional contamination is a phenomenon where the superficial formal overlap between the realisations of two constructions influences the variant distribution of one of the two constructions [@pijpops_constructional_2016; @pijpops_constructional_2018]. The contaminating construction, i.e. the construction that causes the contamination, shows formal overlap with one of the (at least) two realisations of the target construction, i.e. the construction that is being contaminated. Whenever a language user encounters the overlapping form in the contaminating construction, this also inadvertedly boosts the entrenchment [@schmid_entrenchment_2007] of the form in the other construction. As a result, the form that shows overlap with the contaminating construction gains a frequency advantage in the target construction, with the non-overlapping form being used less than expected. The term "constructional contamination" refers to both the cause (the boost process) and the effect (the distributional skew in the target construction) [@pijpops_constructional_2018, 273].

To illustrate constructional contamination, we first discuss the case study from the seminal article by @pijpops_constructional_2016. In this article, @pijpops_constructional_2016 discuss how for two constructions, the partitive genitive (1) and adverb (2) in Dutch, there is superficial overlap between one of the realisations [after @pijpops_constructional_2016, 544-545]:

1. *iets verkeerd(s)* gegeten  
    [something wrong] [eaten]  
2. *iets verkeerd* geïnterpreteerd  
    [something] [wrongly interpreted]

In (1), the partitive genitive, the adjective *verkeerd* 'wrong' modifies the indefinite pronoun *iets* 'something'. In Dutch, the partitive genitive has two realisations: one with *-s*, and one without *-s*.[^standaardtalig-karakter] Because of this, there is overlap between the realisation of the partitive genitive without *-s*, and the adverbal use of an adjective like *verkeerd* 'wrongly', which is always used without *-s*. Note that in (2), *verkeerd* modifies the participle *geïnterpreteerd*, with *iets* serving as the object on its own. Despite the fact that the sequence *iets verkeerd* crosses construction boundaries in (2), @pijpops_constructional_2016 found that the occurrence of *iets verkeerd* in the adverbal construction nonetheless boosts the use of *iets verkeerd* without *-s* in the partitive genitive.

[^standaardtalig-karakter]: According to *Algemene Nederlandse Spraakkunst* [@rys_ans_2024], only the variant with *-s* is standard language, with the status of the *-s*-less variant being unclear.

In addition to the partitive genitive, constructional contamination has also been shown to influence the word order in verbal clusters in Dutch. Verbs *zijn* and *worden* can function as auxiliaries, but also as copula. For example [after @pijpops_constructional_2018, 284-285]:

3. PART + AUX: dat ik door haar vermoeid was  
    that I by her tired was  
    that I was tired by her
4. AUX + PART: dat ik door haar was vermoeid  
    that I by her was tired  
    that I was tired by her
5. ADJ + COP: dat ik heel de dag vermoeid was  
    that I all day tired was  
    that I was tired all day
6. COP + ADJ: \*dat ik heel de dag was vermoeid  
    that I all day was tired
    that I was tired all day

Examples (3) and (4) show the possible word variation between PART + AUX and AUX + PART in verbal clusters. In a predictative copular construction, the same word variation is not possible, with only ADJ + COP being valid. Certain perticiples can also function as adjectives, in which case only the ADJ + COP word order is possible. Because of the formal overlap with the PART + AUX construction, however, @pijpops_constructional_2018 [288] found that whenever a participle is often used as an adjective, the probability of the PART + AUX construction goes up, and we thus see constructional contamination.

Another example also pertains to word order variation in Dutch verbal clusters. @delaby_constructional_2026 show two different constructions in Dutch that use the verb *krijgen* 'to receive'. The receptive construction with *krijgen* (examples 7 and 8) encodes a transfer meaning, while the resultative construction (examples 9 and 10) denotes the result of an action on an object [@delaby_constructional_2026, 2]. The receptive construction allows the same word order variation we saw earlier, while the resultative construction only supports the PART + AUX word order [after @delaby_constructional_2026, 2,4]:

7. PART + AUX: dat we een cadeautje overhandigd kregen  
   that we a present handed got
   that we were handed a present
8. AUX + PART: dat we een cadeautje kregen overhandigd  
   that we a present got handed  
   that we were handed a present
9. PART + AUX: dat we de auto gestart kregen  
    that we the car started got  
    that we got the car started
10. AUX + PART: (?) dat we de auto kregen gestart  
    that we the car got started  
    that we got the car started

@delaby_constructional_2026 found a skew towards the PART + AUX order for verbs that are common to the resultative construction, which is again evidence for constructional contamination.

Our final example comes from English. @hilpert_case_2022 looked at the placement of adverbs in English. The authors discuss the placement of adverbs in passive sentences, where adverbs can appear either in front or behind the participle (examples 11-12). In a noun phrase, however, adverbs can only appear in initial position (examples 13-14) [after @hilpert_case_2022, 284]:

11. Stainless steels are extensively used in petrochemical plants.
12. Stainless steels are used extensively in petrochemical plants.
13. an extensively used technique
14. \*a used extensively technique

Combinations of adverbs and participles that frequently occur as adverb-initial sequences in noun phrases are also more likely to appear as adverb-initial in passive sentences. Here as well, there is contamination from one context to another, in this case from the noun phrase to passive sentences.

The several examples across both Dutch and English show clearly that constructional contamination is a "wide-spread phenomenon" [@pijpops_constructional_2018, 296]. The mechanism behind the contamination process is less clear, however. In this article, we design an agent-based model (ABM) through which we compare two possible explanations for the constructional contamination. The predictions we draw from the ABM, we will then test empirically in a corpus study.

## Explanations for constructional contamination {#sec-explanations}

In order to be able to better reason about the precise mechanism behind constructional constmination, we introduce the formal description used in @pijpops_constructional_2018 [272-275]. On the construction level, we distinguish between the target construction T and the contaminating construction $C$. One variant of the target construction $T$ is $TX$, the other $TY$[^construction-order]. To retain parity with @pijpops_constructional_2018, we assign to $TX$ the variant that shows formal overlap with $C$. As the contaminating construction is restricted to one variant only, it does not have further distinctions. There are also several distinctions on the instance level. In this case, the term "instance" refers to individual lexemes which can appear in both constructions. For the target construction $T$, we use $t_0$ to refer to instances that never show resemblance to the contaminating construction $C$, and $t_1$ to refer to instances that *can* show resemblance to $C$. Of those instances $t_1$, $tx_1$ are the instances of variant $TX$, $ty_1$ are the instances of variant $TY$. To refer to instances of the contaminating construction $C$, we use $c_1$. Constructional contamination is defined as the situation in which instances $t_1$ are skewed in their distribution of $tx_1$ and $ty_1$, with a distributional skew in favour of $tx_1$ compared to $t_0$.

Applied to our example from Dutch, the partitive genitive is the target construction $T$. The variant without *-s* we can refer to as $TX$, the variant with *-s* as $TY$. Since the construction with the adverb influences the partitive genitive construction, it is the contaminating construction $C$. Lexemes that do not show formal overlap between the two constructions are instances $t_0$ (e.g. *leuk*, because it rarely occurs as an adverb). Other lexemes (e.g. *verkeerd*) are instances $t_1$, of which the forms without *-s* are $tx_1$ and the forms without *-s* are $ty_1$. Adverbial instances are always $c_1$.

With these formal definitions, we turn to the possible explanations for constructional contamination. The leading explanation [@pijpops_constructional_2016, 550] points to a combination of shallow parsing [@ferreira_good-enough_2002; @dabrowska_recycling_2014] and chunking [@bybee_language_2010, 76]. Rather than parsing sentences completely and accurately, language users are thought to rely heavily on sequences they have encountered before. As a result, they are assumed to inadvertedly boost the frequency of chunks which are shared with other constructions due coincidental formal overlap. In short, instances of $C$ boost the frequency of a chunk they share with $TX$, which causes constructional contamination within $T$.

Another, simpler explanation solely assumes that in ambiguous sentences, i.e. sentences where the language user cannot reliably distinguish between two constructions, the most likely analysis is chosen according to the frequency counts of both constructions. This implies that instances of $C$ (intended) are sometimes mistaken for $TX$ (understood), which boosts the frequency of $TX$ within $T$ and causes constructional contamination. An important counterargument to this explanation, however, is that instances of $TX$ (intended) can be mistaken for $C$ (understood) just the same, correcting for the boost assumed to help $TX$. In order for the ambiguity-based explanation to work, the boost to $TX$ and the loss to $C$ needs to outweight the boost to $C$, and the loss to $TX$.

In this article, we explore with an agent-based model what contamination behaviour we see when we implement both the chuking-based explanation and the ambiguity-based explanation. For the ambiguity-based explanation specifically, we want to know specificially if and when the boost to $TX$ can outweight the loss to $C$.

## Agent-based simulations

In order to investigate the mechanics behind constructional contamination, we implement two possible explanations using an agent-based model. Agent-based models [@steels_modeling_2011; @ohmer_communication_2025] allow us to program virtual people, also called "agents", in a virtual world. Then, we have these agents communicate with each other according to predefined rules, a step which is often called a "language game" [@smith_models_2014]. Communication between agents is relatively simple, but this is by design. By stripping the model world of the noise typically associated with the real world, we can better focus on the problem at hand [@ohmer_communication_2025, 313], in this case constructional contamination. For us, this means that the vocabulary of the agents as well as their cognitive capacities will be limited to what is relevant for constructional contamination. As a result of the communication between agents, we expect some sort of emergent behaviour to arise, i.e. a boost to $TX$ or to $C$. The big advantage of using an agent-based model for this purpose is that, while the model world is of course simplified, the causality in the small model world is guaranteed. By switching out different parameters in the model (i.e. the frequency distribution between $T$ and $C$, the distribution between $TX$ and $TY$), we can directly assess the impact of different parameter values on the simulation outcome, which in turn allows us to reason about these aspects in the inner workings of constructional contamination.

In the next two sections, we will detail how we built both the chunking-based model and the ambiguity-based model. Both models were implemented using Python and the MESA library [@kazil_utilizing_2020]. Gemma 4 26B A4B[^gemma-link] was used for help with programming (i.e. how to stack vectors in numpy?) and help with the tikz figures, but generated code was never used as-is. All source code is available online.[^github-link]

[^gemma-link]: https://huggingface.co/unsloth/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF/blob/main/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-UD-IQ4_XS.gguf
[^github-link]: https://github.com/AntheSevenants/fwo-frequency-contamination

### Chunking-based model

#### Model design, language game and course of the simulation

First, we discuss the cognitive capabilities of our agents. In the chunking-based explanation, language users are assumed to store frequencies for chunks rather than for individual variants of different constructions (see @sec-explanations). Therefore, in the chunking-basd model, agents can only keep track of the chunk corresponding to $TX$ and $C$, and the chunk corresponding to $TY$. In the case of the Dutch partitive genitive, this would be comparable to the form without *-s* and with *-s* respectively.

Because the decision system in our agent-based models will be Bayesian (see below), we decided not to store frequency counts as-is, but rather as probabilities in a so-called "beliefs system". In the case of the chunking-based model, this means that the preference between the two possible chunks will be stored as probabilities that sum to one. @tbl-agent-memory-chunking shows an example of the probability encoding for an agent in this model. Every agent in the model has their own probabilitiy distribution. Note that, since $C$ can only appear in one variant, the probability sensitivity will not be relevant for the production of $C$.

| Chunk associated with $TX$ and $C$ | Chunk associated with $TY$ |
| --- | --- |
| 0.20 | 0.80 |
: An example of the encoding of the probability of two chunks in the agents' memories in the chunking-based model. {#tbl-agent-memory-chunking}

The $N = 10$ agents in our simulation are initialised with the same beliefs system, which in this case means that all agents share the same initial probability between the two chunks. This division is determined by a parameter $\omega$ ($\ge 0, \lt1$). If $\omega$ is set to $0.2$, the initial beliefs system would correspond to the one shown in @tbl-agent-memory-chunking. Once the model is initialised, agents start conversing with each other, i.e. play the language game. At each model time step, every agent (acting as the speaker) talks to another randomly selected agent (acting as the hearer), in a random order. Due to the random selection procedure, it is possible that certain agents act as hearers multiple times within the same time step. After all agents have had the chance to speak, the agents can converse anew, again in a random order. The more time advances in the model, the more conversations agents thus will have had with each other.

The language game between speaker and hearer occurs as follows. Once speaker and hearer have been selected, the speaker first has to decide whether they will utter construction $T$ or $C$. The probability for this decision is regulated by parameter $\alpha$ ($\ge 0, \lt1$) and remains constant throughout the simulation. Constructional contamination does not prescribe that the probability of uttering, say, a partitive genitive or adverb changes as a result of formal overlap. The need to utter a specific construction emanates from the real world, and we assume this need remains constant despite potential contamination. If $\alpha$ is set to $0.6$, then agents will utter construction $T$ in 60% of cases. If the speaker chooses to utter construction $C$, they cannot choose between variants, so they always utter the chunk associated with both $C$ and $TX$. If the speaker chooses to utter construction $T$, they have the choice between that same chunk corresponding to $C$ or $TX$, or the chunk corresponding to $TY$. The choice between the two chunks is made based on the probabilities of the beliefs system exemplified in @tbl-agent-memory-chunking. The chosen chunk is then communicated to the hearer.

Next, the hearer "hears" the utterance made by the speaker. In the chunking-based model, no disambiguation is necessary, so the hearer only has to update their beliefs system according to what they just heard. The update mechanism works according to an Exponential Moving Average. For example, if the hearer hears the chunk associated with $TY$, we generate a new probability for the chunk of $TY$ according to @eq-update:

$$
\begin{aligned}
  &x_\text{observed} \in \{0, 1\} \\
  &p_{new} = p_{old} + \lambda(x_t - p_{old})
  \end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-update}

In this case, we observe a probability $1$ for chunk $TY$ ($x_\text{observed}$). We generate a new probability $p_{new}$ based on the sum of the old probability $p_{old}$ and the difference with the observed probability $x_\text{observed}$, multiplied by a learning rate $\lambda$. $\lambda$ controls how fast the beliefs of an agent update when they encounter a chunk. To keep the behaviour of the agents stable, we decided to pin $\lambda$ at $0.01$. Conversely, if the agent observed the chunk associated with $TY$, they did not observe the other chunk associated with $TX$ and $C$, so its probability is updated with observed probability $0$.

#### Results and evaluation

As we discussed earlier, computer simulations allow us to reason about causality within the model world. In order to estimate the influence of the different parameters, we varied the parameters shown in @tbl-chunking-parameters in the simulation.

| Parameter | Explanation | Values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\alpha$ | Probability of $T$. Probability of $C$ is $1 - \alpha$ | $0.2$, $0.4$, $0.5$, $0.6$, $0.8$ |
| $\omega$| Probability of $TX$. Probability of $TY$ is $1 - \omega$ | $0.0$, $0.2$, $0.4$, $0.5$, $0.6$, $0.8$|
: An overview of all parameters in the simulation and their values, for the chunking-based model. {#tbl-chunking-parameters}

Due to the probabilistic nature of the simulation, we tested every unique combination of parameters 100 times. In all model behaviour graphs in this article, we show an aggregation across these 100 runs for each combination. For each combination, we show the median, and the interquartile range Q1 and Q3.

- Voorstelling model.
- Resultaten.
- Voorspelling: des te vaker een woord voorkomt in de C en des te minder vaak in T, des te vaker de -s wegvalt.

### Ambiguity-based model

#### Model design, language game and course of the simulation

The beliefs system for the ambiguity-based model is more intricate, since in the ambiguity-based model, agents do not store chunks. Rather, agents are sensitive to the probability of both $T$ and $C$, and separately to the probability of $TX$ and $TY$. The initial sensitivity to $T$ and $C$ is taken from parameter $\alpha$, but can change over time. Here as well, the initial distribution between $TX$ and $TY$ is regulated by parameter $\omega$. If $\alpha$ is set to $0.2$, and $\omega$ to $0.7$, the initial beliefs system would correspond to the one shown in @tbl-agent-memory-ambiguity.

| Construction $T$ | | Construction $C$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.2 | 0.8 ||
| Construction $TX$ | Construction $TY$ | ^^ |
| 0.7 | 0.3 | 1 |
: An example of the encoding of the probability of constructions $T$ and $C$, and $TX$ and $TY$ in the ambiguity-based model. {#tbl-agent-memory-ambiguity}

The language game played by speaker and hearer also differs from the one in the chuking-based model. First, the speaker still has to decide whether to utter construction $T$ or $C$, a choice which remains regulated by parameter $\alpha$. If $T$ was chosen, the speaker further chooses between $TX$ and $TY$ based on the stored probabilities. If $C$ was chosen, no such choice is made.

Finally, at the start of each conversation, it is determined whether the utterance made by the speaker will be of ambiguous nature. This is not a decision made by the speaker, but rather again a property that we assume arises organically from some situation in the real world. In order to be able to assess the influence of ambiguity on constructional contamination, we define ambiguity parameter $\epsilon$, with separate ambiguity values for $TX$ and $C$. If $\epsilon_{TX}$ = $0.5$, 50% of $TX$ utterances will be ambiguous. Since $TY$ by definition is a distinct construction without formal overlap, this construction will never be ambiguous.

Next, the hearer again "hears" the utterance made by the speaker. If the utterance is unambiguous, probabilities at both the construction and variant level are immediately updated according to @eq-update. If the utterance is ambiguous (i.e. because $TX$ or $C$ were uttered), the hearer first runs a Bayesian maximum likelihood estimation (shown in @eq-bayesian) to decide which construction was most likely intended. The construction with the highest probability[^bayes-note] is chosen as the heard construction.

[^bayes-note]: Technically speaking, we skip part of the Bayesian equation by not calculating the denominator $p(\text{overlap variant})$. This makes our formulas compute a score rather than a probability. The division operation is superfluous, because it is equal across the two computations (hence the operator $\propto$).

$$
\begin{aligned}
  &p(TX \mid \text{overlap variant}) \propto p(\text{overlap variant} \mid T) \cdot p(T) \\
  &p(C \mid \text{overlap variant}) \propto p(\text{overlap variant} \mid C) \cdot p(C)
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-bayesian}

#### Results and evaluation

For this model as well, we varied several parameters, given in @tbl-ambiguity-parameters. All possible combinations were tested 100 times.

| Parameter | Explanation | Values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\alpha$ | Probability of $T$. Probability of $C$ is $1 - \alpha$ | $0.2$, $0.4$, $0.5$, $0.6$, $0.8$ |
| $\omega$| Probability of $TX$. Probability of $TY$ is $1 - \omega$ | $0.0$, $0.2$, $0.4$, $0.5$, $0.6$, $0.8$|
| $\epsilon_{TX}$ | Ambiguity of utterances with construction $TX$. | $0.2$, $0.8$ |
| $\epsilon_{C}$ | Ambiguity of utterances with construction $C$. | $0.2$, $0.8$ |
: An overview of all parameters in the simulation and their values, for the ambiguity-based model. {#tbl-ambiguity-parameters}

- Resultaten.
- De ‘boost’ weegt harder door dan het ‘verlies’ wanneer het lexeem in kwestie frequenter is in TX dan in C. Het ‘verlies’ weegt harder door dan de ‘boost’ wanneer het lexeem in kwestie frequenter is in C dan in TX. Dat leidt tot de volgende voorspellingen
    - Bij lexemen waar TX frequenter is dan C verwachten we sterkere constructionele contaminatie dan bij lexemen waar C frequenter is dan TX
    - In Nederland verwachten we minder constructionele contaminatie dan in België omdat TX daar zo onbekend is (bij de partitieve genitief)[DP2.1]
